# Time series {#lagoa-time-series}

The annual maps form a 40-year series for each class. `land_time_series()`
extracts the series of interest, here soybean (39), pasture (15) and forest
formation (3):

```{r series, fig.height=5}
series <- land_time_series(areas$time_series, classes = c(39, 15, 3),
                           language = "en")
series$plot
```

## Association between two series {-}

Two trending series often look related even when they have nothing to do with
each other from one year to the next. That is why `series_correlation()` can
measure association on the levels, on the annual differences or on the
residuals of a trend, and corrects the p-value for autocorrelation:

```{r correlation, fig.height=4.5}
correlation <- series_correlation(series, 39, 15, transformation = "difference",
                                  language = "en")
correlation$plots$association
```

```{r include=FALSE}
assoc <- correlation$association
```

On annual differences, the correlation between soybean and pasture is
r = `r num(assoc$estimate, 2)` (p = `r num(assoc$p_value, 2)`; corrected p =
`r num(assoc$p_serial, 2)`). In other words, the replacement of one class by the
other is clear in the levels, over several years, but their year-to-year
changes do not move together.

## Regimes and change points {-}

`series_fit_regime()` fits a continuous curve with transitions between regimes.
The probabilistic bent-cable model estimates when each transition happens and
how long it lasts, with bootstrap confidence intervals:

```{r regime, fig.height=5.5}
fit <- series_fit_regime(series, 39, model = "prob_bent_logistic",
                         bootstrap = 200, seed = 1, language = "en")
fit$plot
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
pc <- fit$change_points
tabela(data.frame(Transition = pc$transition, Year = pc$estimate, `95% CI lower` = pc$conf_low,
                  `95% CI upper` = pc$conf_high, `Rate before (km²/yr)` = pc$slope_before,
                  `Rate after (km²/yr)` = pc$slope_after, check.names = FALSE), 2)
```

The soybean story has three transitions, all between `r floor(min(pc$estimate))`
and `r ceiling(max(pc$estimate))`: first a rapid expansion of
`r num(pc$slope_after[1], 1)` km² per year, then a contraction and, from
`r round(pc$estimate[3])` on, slow growth. With `model = "auto"`, the function
compares the available models by AICc and picks the most suitable one.

## Diagnostics and projection {-}

```{r diagnostics, fig.height=4}
diagnostics <- series_diagnostics(fit)
diagnostics$plots$acf
```

```{r include=FALSE}
q <- diagnostics$quality
```

The fit explains `r num(100 * q$r_squared, 0)`% of the variation (R²), but the
residuals are autocorrelated (Durbin-Watson = `r num(q$durbin_watson, 2)`;
Ljung-Box, `r if (q$ljung_box_p_value < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else paste("p =", num(q$ljung_box_p_value, 3))`).
When residuals depend on each other, intervals tend to come out too narrow. In
that case, `bootstrap_type = "block"` resamples blocks of consecutive years and
produces more realistic intervals.

Finally, `series_forecast()` extends the last regime:

```{r projection, fig.height=4.5}
projection <- series_forecast(fit, horizon = 5)
projection$plot
```

The projection assumes the current regime continues. Read it as a scenario,
not as a prediction of future land use change.
